items.readable_text:
Content:
Given an integer [MATH: a,] the residue class (or congruence class) of [MATH: a] modulo [MATH: n] is the set containing all integers congruent to [MATH: a] (modulo [MATH: n]).

Content:
The residue class of [MATH: a] modulo [MATH: n,] denoted [MATH: [a]_n,] can be expressed using a conditional definition as follows:

Content:
[MATH: [a]_n = \big\{ x \in \mathbb{Z} \: | \: x \equiv a \, \: (\text{mod}\:n) \big\}]

Content:
Put another way, the residue class [MATH: [a]_n] contains all integers that have the same remainder as [MATH: a] when divided by [MATH: n.]

Content:
For example, the residue class of [MATH: 0] modulo [MATH: 2] contains all the even integers because they all have a remainder of zero when divided by [MATH: 2.]

Content:
[MATH: [0]_{2}|= {x ∈ Z|x≡0(mod2)}; = {2k|k ∈ Z}; = {…, − 4, − 2, 0, 2, 4…}]

Content:
The residue class of [MATH: 1] modulo [MATH: 2] contains all the odd integers because they all have a remainder of one when divided by [MATH: 2.]

Content:
[MATH: [1]_{2}|= {x ∈ Z|x≡1(mod2)}; = {2k + 1|k ∈ Z}; = {…, − 3, − 1, 1, 3, 5…}]

Content:
Note that each element of [MATH: \mathbb Z] lies either in [MATH: [0]_2] or in [MATH: [1]_2] (but never both). Thus, these residue classes form a partition of the integers. We'll call this partition [MATH: \mathbb Z_2{:}]

Content:
[MATH: \mathbb Z_2 = \big\{[0]_2, [1]_2\big\}]

Content:
We can visualize this partition using the diagram shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/ce5339059df52ad5cb6f5ade2da139d5]

Content:
Similarly, the integers can also be partitioned into five residue classes modulo [MATH: 5.]

Content:
[MATH: \mathbb Z_5 = \big\{[0]_5, [1]_5, [2]_5,[3]_5, [4]_5 \big\}]

Content:
In this case, each residue class contains all numbers that are congruent modulo [MATH: 5.] We can visualize this partition of [MATH: \mathbb Z] using the diagram below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/576e698e54d4c9a47027bb04c5733108]

Content:
A residue class is a specific type of a more general object called an equivalence class. We'll learn more about different types of equivalence classes soon.

Content:
Let's go back to our diagram for visualizing the residue classes modulo [MATH: 2.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/51418213a2aa85a5e6d16db776c20453]

Content:
Any given representation of a residue class is not unique.

Content:
For example, the integers congruent to zero modulo [MATH: 2] are usually denoted [MATH: [0]_2.] In this case, [MATH: 0] is the representative of the class:
[MATH: [0]_{2} = {x|x≡0(mod2)}]

Content:
However, we can use any element of the class to represent the class. Here are some examples:

Content:
[MATH: [2]_{2}|= {x|x≡2(mod2)}; [4]_{2}|= {x|x≡4(mod2)}; [6]_{2}|= {x|x≡6(mod2)}; ⋮]

Content:
We can also use negative numbers as representatives of the class:

Content:
[MATH: [− 2]_{2}|= {x|x≡ − 2(mod2)}; [− 4]_{2}|= {x|x≡ − 4(mod2)}; [− 6]_{2}|= {x|x≡ − 6(mod2)}; ⋮]

Content:
What's important to understand is that all of these sets are equal:

Content:
[MATH: [0]_{2}|= [2]_{2} = [4]_{2} = [6]_{2} = ⋯; = [− 2]_{2} = [− 4]_{2} = [− 6]_{2} = ⋯]

Content:
The same idea is true for [MATH: [1]_2{:}]

Content:
[MATH: [1]_{2}|= [3]_{2} = [5]_{2} = [7]_{2} = ⋯; = [− 1]_{2} = [− 3]_{2} = [− 5]_{2} = ⋯]

Content:
The same idea applies to any residue class modulo [MATH: n.] For example:

Content:
[MATH: [0]_{5}|= [5]_{5} = [10]_{5} = ⋯; [1]_{5}|= [6]_{5} = [11]_{5} = ⋯; [2]_{5}|= [7]_{5} = [12]_{5} = ⋯; [3]_{5}|= [8]_{5} = [13]_{5} = ⋯; [4]_{5}|= [9]_{5} = [15]_{5} = ⋯]

Content:
Despite this non-uniqueness, we usually choose the smallest nonnegative element of a residue class to represent the class.

sections.normalized_html:
Which of the following integers belong to the residue class [MATH: [5]_{8}?]

  1. [MATH: -3]

  2. [MATH: 13]

Which of the following integers belong to the residue class [MATH: [5]_{8}?]

2. [MATH: 13]
3. [MATH: 3]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The residue class [MATH: [5]_{8}] consists of the elements that are congruent to [MATH: 5] modulo [MATH: 8.] So, we have

[MATH: [5]_{8}|= {x ∈ Z|x≡5(mod8)}; = {x ∈ Z|x = 5 + 8k, k ∈ Z}; = {5 + 8k|k ∈ Z}; = {…, 5 − 2 ⋅ 8, 5 − 8, 5, 5 + 8, 5 + 2 ⋅ 8, …}; = {…, − 11, − 3, 5, 13, 21, …}.]

We see that [MATH: -3] and [MATH: 13] belong to [MATH: [5]_{8},] while [MATH: 3] does not.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

items.title: Properties of Residue Classes

sections.normalized_html: Let's list some important properties of residue classes:
sections.readable_text: Let's list some important properties of residue classes:

sections.normalized_html:
• There are exactly [MATH: n] distinct residue classes modulo [MATH: n.]

  • If [MATH: a \equiv b \: (\text{mod}\:n)] then [MATH: [a]_n=[b]_n.] In particular, this allows us to pick any element of a class as its representative.

  • On the other hand, two distinct residue classes have an empty intersection: [MATH: a \not\equiv b \quad (\text{mod}\:n) \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad [a]_n \cap [b]_n = \emptyset]

  • The residue classes modulo [MATH: n] form a partition of the set of all integers. This means the integers can be constructed from the (disjoint) union of all distinct residue classes. [MATH: \mathbb{Z} = [0]_n \cup [1]_n \cup \cdots \cup [n-1]_n]

sections.normalized_html:
If [MATH: [a]_n] denotes the residue class containing all integers congruent to [MATH: a] modulo [MATH: n,] then which of the following residue classes is equal to [MATH: [13]_3?]

  1. [MATH: [0]_3]

  2. [MATH: [1]_3]

  3. [MATH: [2]_3]
sections.readable_text:
If [MATH: [a]_n] denotes the residue class containing all integers congruent to [MATH: a] modulo [MATH: n,] then which of the following residue classes is equal to [MATH: [13]_3?]

1. [MATH: [0]_3]
2. [MATH: [1]_3]
3. [MATH: [2]_3]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
We have [MATH: [a]_{3} = [b]_{3}] if [MATH: a \equiv b \quad (\text{mod}\:3).]

The residue class [MATH: [13]_{3}] consists of the elements that are congruent to [MATH: 13] modulo [MATH: 3.]

We can find an alternative representation for this residue class as follows:

[MATH: [13]_{3}|= {x ∈ Z|x≡13(mod3)}; = {x ∈ Z|x≡4 ⋅ 3 + 1(mod3)}; = {x ∈ Z|x≡4 ⋅ 0 + 1(mod3)}; = {x ∈ Z|x≡1(mod3)}; = [1]_{3}.]

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only".
sections.readable_text:
We have [MATH: [a]_{3} = [b]_{3}] if
[MATH: a \equiv b \quad (\text{mod}\:3).]

The residue class [MATH: [13]_{3}] consists of the elements that are congruent to [MATH: 13] modulo [MATH: 3.]

[MATH: [13]_{3}|= {x ∈ Z|x≡13(mod3)}; = {x ∈ Z|x≡4 ⋅ 3 + 1(mod3)}; = {x ∈ Z|x≡4 ⋅ 0 + 1(mod3)}; = {x ∈ Z|x≡1(mod3)}; = [1]_{3}.]

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only".

  • Statement II is true. Indeed, since [MATH: 5 \not\equiv 9 \: (\text{mod }3),] we have that [MATH: [5]_3\cap [9]_3= \emptyset.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Given an integer [MATH: a,] the residue class (or congruence class) of [MATH: a] modulo [MATH: n] is the set containing all integers congruent to [MATH: a] (modulo [MATH: n]).

Content:
The residue class of [MATH: a] modulo [MATH: n,] denoted [MATH: [a]_n,] can be expressed using a conditional definition as follows:

Content:
[MATH: [a]_n = \big\{ x \in \mathbb{Z} \: | \: x \equiv a \, \: (\text{mod}\:n) \big\}]

Content:
Put another way, the residue class [MATH: [a]_n] contains all integers that have the same remainder as [MATH: a] when divided by [MATH: n.]

Content:
For example, the residue class of [MATH: 0] modulo [MATH: 2] contains all the even integers because they all have a remainder of zero when divided by [MATH: 2.]

Content:
[MATH: [0]_{2}|= {x ∈ Z|x≡0(mod2)}; = {2k|k ∈ Z}; = {…, − 4, − 2, 0, 2, 4…}]

Content:
The residue class of [MATH: 1] modulo [MATH: 2] contains all the odd integers because they all have a remainder of one when divided by [MATH: 2.]

Content:
[MATH: [1]_{2}|= {x ∈ Z|x≡1(mod2)}; = {2k + 1|k ∈ Z}; = {…, − 3, − 1, 1, 3, 5…}]

Content:
Note that each element of [MATH: \mathbb Z] lies either in [MATH: [0]_2] or in [MATH: [1]_2] (but never both). Thus, these residue classes form a partition of the integers. We'll call this partition [MATH: \mathbb Z_2{:}]

Content:
[MATH: \mathbb Z_2 = \big\{[0]_2, [1]_2\big\}]

Content:
We can visualize this partition using the diagram shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/ce5339059df52ad5cb6f5ade2da139d5]

Content:
Similarly, the integers can also be partitioned into five residue classes modulo [MATH: 5.]

Content:
[MATH: \mathbb Z_5 = \big\{[0]_5, [1]_5, [2]_5,[3]_5, [4]_5 \big\}]

Content:
In this case, each residue class contains all numbers that are congruent modulo [MATH: 5.] We can visualize this partition of [MATH: \mathbb Z] using the diagram below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/576e698e54d4c9a47027bb04c5733108]

Content:
A residue class is a specific type of a more general object called an equivalence class. We'll learn more about different types of equivalence classes soon.

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: Representatives

Content:
Let's go back to our diagram for visualizing the residue classes modulo [MATH: 2.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/51418213a2aa85a5e6d16db776c20453]

Content:
Any given representation of a residue class is not unique.

Content:
For example, the integers congruent to zero modulo [MATH: 2] are usually denoted [MATH: [0]_2.] In this case, [MATH: 0] is the representative of the class:
[MATH: [0]_{2} = {x|x≡0(mod2)}]

Content:
However, we can use any element of the class to represent the class. Here are some examples:

Content:
[MATH: [2]_{2}|= {x|x≡2(mod2)}; [4]_{2}|= {x|x≡4(mod2)}; [6]_{2}|= {x|x≡6(mod2)}; ⋮]

Content:
We can also use negative numbers as representatives of the class:

Content:
[MATH: [− 2]_{2}|= {x|x≡ − 2(mod2)}; [− 4]_{2}|= {x|x≡ − 4(mod2)}; [− 6]_{2}|= {x|x≡ − 6(mod2)}; ⋮]

Content:
What's important to understand is that all of these sets are equal:

Content:
[MATH: [0]_{2}|= [2]_{2} = [4]_{2} = [6]_{2} = ⋯; = [− 2]_{2} = [− 4]_{2} = [− 6]_{2} = ⋯]

Content:
The same idea is true for [MATH: [1]_2{:}]

Content:
[MATH: [1]_{2}|= [3]_{2} = [5]_{2} = [7]_{2} = ⋯; = [− 1]_{2} = [− 3]_{2} = [− 5]_{2} = ⋯]

Content:
The same idea applies to any residue class modulo [MATH: n.] For example:

Content:
[MATH: [0]_{5}|= [5]_{5} = [10]_{5} = ⋯; [1]_{5}|= [6]_{5} = [11]_{5} = ⋯; [2]_{5}|= [7]_{5} = [12]_{5} = ⋯; [3]_{5}|= [8]_{5} = [13]_{5} = ⋯; [4]_{5}|= [9]_{5} = [15]_{5} = ⋯]

Content:
Despite this non-uniqueness, we usually choose the smallest nonnegative element of a residue class to represent the class.

---

Item 3 — Example: Identifying Elements Belonging to a Residue Class

Example Prompt:
Which of the following integers belong to the residue class [MATH: [5]_{8}?]

1. [MATH: -3]
2. [MATH: 13]
3. [MATH: 3]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The residue class [MATH: [5]_{8}] consists of the elements that are congruent to [MATH: 5] modulo [MATH: 8.] So, we have

[MATH: [5]_{8}|= {x ∈ Z|x≡5(mod8)}; = {x ∈ Z|x = 5 + 8k, k ∈ Z}; = {5 + 8k|k ∈ Z}; = {…, 5 − 2 ⋅ 8, 5 − 8, 5, 5 + 8, 5 + 2 ⋅ 8, …}; = {…, − 11, − 3, 5, 13, 21, …}.]

We see that [MATH: -3] and [MATH: 13] belong to [MATH: [5]_{8},] while [MATH: 3] does not.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

[MATH: 7 \equiv a \quad (\text{mod}\:3).]

Let's now consider each of the given equivalence classes.

- [MATH: 7 \in [4]_3] because [MATH: 7 \equiv 4 \: (\text{mod}\:3)] [MATH: \quad \color{green}\checkmark]
- [MATH: 7 \not\in [-1]_3] because [MATH: 7 \not\equiv -1 \: (\text{mod}\:3)] [MATH: \quad \color{red}\times]
- [MATH: 7 \in [1]_3] because [MATH: 7 \equiv 1 \: (\text{mod}\:3)] [MATH: \quad \color{green}\checkmark]

Item 9 — Tutorial: Properties of Residue Classes

Content:
Let's list some important properties of residue classes:

Content:
- There are exactly [MATH: n] distinct residue classes modulo [MATH: n.]
- If [MATH: a \equiv b \: (\text{mod}\:n)] then [MATH: [a]_n=[b]_n.] In particular, this allows us to pick any element of a class as its representative.
- On the other hand, two distinct residue classes have an empty intersection:
[MATH: a \not\equiv b \quad (\text{mod}\:n)
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
[a]_n \cap [b]_n = \emptyset]
- The residue classes modulo [MATH: n] form a partition of the set of all integers. This means the integers can be constructed from the (disjoint) union of all distinct residue classes.
[MATH: \mathbb{Z} = [0]_n \cup [1]_n \cup \cdots \cup [n-1]_n]

Content:
The integers modulo [MATH: \boldsymbol n] is defined as the set containing all distinct residue classes modulo [MATH: n]: [MATH: \mathbb{Z}_n = \big\{[0]_n,\, [1]_n,\, \ldots,\, [n-1]_n\big\}]

Content:
The set [MATH: \mathbb Z_n] has some interesting properties. We'll learn more about those in future lessons.

---

Item 10 — Example: Identifying Equivalent Residue Classes

Example Prompt:
If [MATH: [a]_n] denotes the residue class containing all integers congruent to [MATH: a] modulo [MATH: n,] then which of the following residue classes is equal to [MATH: [13]_3?]

1. [MATH: [0]_3]
2. [MATH: [1]_3]
3. [MATH: [2]_3]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We have [MATH: [a]_{3} = [b]_{3}] if
[MATH: a \equiv b \quad (\text{mod}\:3).]

The residue class [MATH: [13]_{3}] consists of the elements that are congruent to [MATH: 13] modulo [MATH: 3.]

We can find an alternative representation for this residue class as follows:

[MATH: [13]_{3}|= {x ∈ Z|x≡13(mod3)}; = {x ∈ Z|x≡4 ⋅ 3 + 1(mod3)}; = {x ∈ Z|x≡4 ⋅ 0 + 1(mod3)}; = {x ∈ Z|x≡1(mod3)}; = [1]_{3}.]

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only".
